InteroceptomicsExperiment guide

What changes around a heartbeat?

Skin electrodes pick up the heart’s electrical activity. A second sensor records tiny chest vibrations, and a band follows breathing. All three instruments recorded at the same time while a person lay still.

Opening the archived recording…

Each trace has its own vertical scale in millivolts (mV), the voltage reported by that sensor. Tap a trace or move the time slider to compare the same sample across all three.

Interoception is sensing what is happening inside your body. These recordings give an outside measurement of three changes the body undergoes. There is no sensory-nerve recording or participant report of a felt heartbeat here.

What and when did the instruments measure?

Two ECG leads record the heart’s electrical activity from different directions. The breathing band and chest accelerometer each report an electrical output related to motion. The stored voltages do not provide lung volume, muscle force, blood pressure or a calibrated acceleration in this viewer.

Each excerpt runs from 60.0000 through 71.9998 seconds on a 5,000-sample-per-second clock. The step between samples is 0.2 ms. A visible ECG mark is the archive’s beat label for that lead. The archive does not identify a particular valve movement or a time when the person felt a beat.

At screen widths narrower than the recording, each drawn column includes the lowest and highest samples within it. The numeric readout always uses the original row.
